passage:
I sit two desks from Ira and across the aisle from Pema, so I saw most of it. Only one team-lead seat was open, and both of them wanted it.

For a week they moved like allies pretending to be neutral. Then I noticed a change. Ira started sending Pema the client's updated file, unasked, with a line like "in case it helps the deck." Pema returned the favour by sharing the pricing sheet. They both worked late, and their slides got much sharper.

Ira didn't win. On the day the email came, Pema walked over to Ira's desk and said, "Your risk slide was better than mine." Ira answered, "Congrats. I'll take the next one."

Maybe they weren't friends. But nobody hid information, and they still eat lunch at the same table. My name is Deepak, by the way.

qa.q: How many team-lead seats were open?
qa.a: Only one team-lead seat was open.

qa.q: What does Ira's sending of the updated client file suggest about Ira's attitude?
qa.a: It suggests Ira was confident enough to compete through strong work rather than by hiding information, though Deepak cannot be sure what Ira privately felt.

qa.q: What made this rivalry healthy rather than harmful?
qa.a: Both shared useful files, kept courtesy, and accepted the result without spite, so the competition sharpened their slides instead of breaking trust.

qa.q: How might Deepak, watching from the aisle, see the two rivals?
qa.a: Deepak sees two colleagues who compete but still respect each other; Deepak cannot tell if they are friends, only that no one sabotaged anyone.

grounding: Two colleagues compete for one seat; an observer shows healthy rivalry with shared information and a gracious loss.

passage:
Only one of them would be made duty manager at the Grand Residency hotel in Jaipur, and Gautam and Siddharth both knew it. They had been friends since the training batch. Now they barely spoke at the front desk.
On Tuesday a message came through for Siddharth: the German tour group was arriving three hours early. Gautam read it first. For a moment he thought of letting Siddharth find out late. It would look bad for him.
Gautam's stomach twisted. Then he walked to the back office. "Sid, your German group's coming at eleven, not two. I've blocked the rooms on the third floor."
Siddharth stared at him. "Thanks, yaar."
Two weeks later the post went to Siddharth. Gautam shook his hand in the lobby. "You'll be good at it." He meant it, mostly. The rest he could sort out on his own time.

qa.q: When was the German tour group arriving?
qa.a: At eleven, three hours early, instead of two.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when he first read the message?
qa.a: He felt tempted and tense, briefly wanting his rival to look bad, and his stomach twisted at the thought.

qa.q: What made Gautam's rivalry healthy rather than harmful?
qa.a: He passed on the information and helped with the rooms instead of hiding it, and when he lost, he congratulated Siddharth without spite.

qa.q: How might Siddharth see Gautam after the tour-group message?
qa.a: Siddharth is likely grateful and a little surprised, seeing that Gautam stayed a friend even while competing.

grounding: Two colleagues compete for one post; the protagonist shares vital information instead of hiding it, and loses without spite.

passage:
Subject: Handover notes for the regional role
Dear Gurleen,
Congratulations on the regional coordinator role. I won't pretend I wasn't hoping for it too; you know I was. For a few weeks there, I think we both stopped sharing things in team meetings, and I'm not proud of my part in that.
I'm attaching my notes on the three district partners I've been working with, including the contact at the Bathinda office who only answers after four. I'd rather you start strong than learn that the hard way.
Competing with you made my own proposal sharper than it would have been. That part I'm grateful for.
If you need anything from my side, just ask. I'm around.
Warmly,
Sabina

qa.q: What does Sabina attach to the email?
qa.a: Notes on the three district partners, including the Bathinda contact who only answers after four.

qa.q: What does Sabina admit feeling during the competition?
qa.a: Sabina admits hoping for the role and feeling not proud of withholding things in meetings, which shows some regret.

qa.q: How does Sabina lose the rivalry well?
qa.a: By congratulating Gurleen honestly, sharing useful handover notes, and offering support instead of spite.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel on receiving these notes?
qa.a: Gurleen may feel relieved and grateful, and the rivalry may soften back into a working friendship.

grounding: After a rivalry for one post, the protagonist loses without spite, shares useful information, and credits the rivalry for sharpening the work.
